input: The conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methanol over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst is a reaction of considerable practical interest, and the form in which the catalyst is deployed can matter as much as the chemistry itself. This study sets the two forms side by side on one feed composition. Space-time yield, in this context, is the mass of product formed per unit catalyst volume per hour. The tests themselves were carried out at 250 °C and 50 bar with feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 0.88 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 9% after 100 h. The extruded pellet, by contrast, gave 0.32 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.57 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Read together, the figures paint a consistent picture: under the conditions tested, the monolith produced more methanol per unit volume, imposed a smaller resistance on the flowing gas, and gave up a smaller share of its activity over the test period than the pellet form did. That picture, however, comes with boundaries that should be kept firmly in view. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested at any point, and it is also the case that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes comparisons of this kind harder to assemble than they might appear.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol, and two catalyst forms are compared on one feed composition. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour. The tests ran at 250 °C and 50 bar with feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 0.88 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 9% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gave 0.32 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.57 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. The monolith has the higher yield, the lower pressure drop, and the smaller activity loss under the stated conditions. The ranking is a ranking of the two forms as charged and tested; it is not a ranking of the catalyst material in other forms or on other feeds. Pressure drop is stated for the catalyst charge as tested, and the activity losses are stated at the end of the same test period for both forms. The comparison is limited to the stated feed composition, temperature, and pressure. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the comparison inherits that limit. The three measures describe the same charges under the same conditions, and all three favour the same form. No measure in the set runs against the ranking the other two give.
